rp-fire-02.back: Grass, herbs and fireweed under the snags. Elk and bears graze.

rp-fire-03.back: Shrubs and aspen root suckers: peak browse for deer and moose.

rp-fire-04.back: Dense young forest: hiding cover, less food.

rp-fire-05.front: Which seeds germinate in response to fire?

rp-fire-06.front: How does aspen come back after fire?
rp-fire-06.back: Root suckers that quickly form a dense shrub layer.

rp-fire-07.back: Moose used low and medium severity patches, especially wet sites.

rp-fire-08.front: Elk use of a prescribed burn over time (Montana)?
rp-fire-08.back: Up in years 1 to 2, then back to normal over 3 to 10 years.

rp-fire-09.back: Most break or fall in the first 15 years; few in the first 5.

rp-fire-10.back: Danger trees, hidden hot ash pits, floods and debris flows, unstable slopes and rockfall.

rp-fire-11.front: How long can post fire risks last?
rp-fire-11.back: 2 years or more in severely burned areas.

rp-fire-12.back: Park and camp in the open, more than a tree length from any snag.

rp-fire-13.back: Area restrictions, possible season closures, and new fireguard roads.

rp-fire-14.front: Best place to hunt in a burn?
rp-fire-14.back: Edges between unburned islands and burned feed.
